content: Now it turns out that for the last eight years, another major book was in the works: "W. E. B. Du Bois: Biography of a Race, 1868-1919" (Henry Holt & Company, New York, $35), a 735-page tome, described by Dr. Lewis in his preface as a project that "often rendered me unaware of the routine of daily life." Du Bois died in 1963 at the age of 95, and the research involved travel over three continents, inquiry into 28 archives and 99 library collections and interviews with more than 150 people. "And alas," Dr. Lewis said recently, "all this for what it turns out is only volume one." But "Du Bois" -- a candidate for the National Book Award in nonfiction -- is a powerfully thorough book that because its subject was such a extraordinary leader, so central to the political controversies around him, it compels a reappraisal of the post-Civil War era. Du Bois is perhaps best known in the civil rights movement for his insistence on full equality for his fellow blacks, as opposed to the accommodative policies of Booker T. Washington. But Dr. Lewis's book reveals much more about Du Bois as political strategist. In 1911, for example, when Woodrow Wilson, then Governor of New Jersey, prepared to enter the Presidential race, he asked Du Bois to influence blacks to depart from their traditional Republican stance and vote Democratic. After Wilson won with a larger-than-expected vote and segregationist politics continued, Du Bois retaliated with searing anti-Wilson editorials in The Crisis, the magazine of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People.

**Justification:** The passage explicitly states that Du Bois was an "extraordinary leader" and details his involvement in political strategy, including influencing voting patterns and engaging in public commentary through "The Crisis" magazine. The term “abolition-democracy” began with Du Bois and is worth further exploration. Abolition-democracy, Du Bois writes, was the “liberal movement among both laborers and small capitalists” who saw “the danger of slavery to both capital and labor.” Its standard-bearers were abolitionists like Wendell Phillips and radical antislavery politicians like Charles Sumner and Thaddeus Stevens, and in its eyes, “the only real object” of the Civil War was the abolition of slavery and “it was convinced that this could be thoroughly accomplished only if the emancipated Negroes became free citizens and voters.” It was also clear to some within abolition-democracy that “freedom in order to be free required a minimum of capital in addition to political rights.” In this way, abolition-democracy was an anticipation of social democratic ideology, although few of its proponents, in Du Bois’s view, grasped the full significance of their analysis of the relationship between political freedom, civil rights and economic security. Opposing abolition-democracy, in Du Bois’s telling, were the reactionaries of the former Confederate South who sought to “re-establish slavery by force.” The South, he writes, “opposed Negro education, opposed land and capital for Negroes, and violently and bitterly opposed any political power. It fought every conception inch by inch: no real emancipation, limited civil rights, no Negro schools, no votes for Negroes.” Between these two sides lay Northern industry and capital. It wanted profits and it would join whichever force enabled it to expand its power and reach. Initially, this meant abolition-democracy, as Northern industry feared the return of a South that might threaten its political and economic dominance. It “swung inevitably toward democracy” rather than allow the “continuation of Southern oligarchy,” Du Bois writes.

**Justification:** The passage discusses Du Bois's intellectual contributions, specifically his concept of "abolition-democracy."
